content: 1. Further diuresis should only be undertaken with careful monitoring of renal function to avoid potential complications. 2. Patients should weigh themselves every morning at the same time using the same scale, and diuretic dosing should be adjusted to maintain a stable weight. 3. Due to the risk of hypokalemia or hyperkalemia, blood electrolyte levels should be checked regularly. 4. After initiating diuretics, or simultaneously with their initiation, an ACE inhibitor can be started. 5. ACE inhibitors include drugs such as enalapril, ramipril, quinapril, perindopril, lisinopril, and benazepril. 6. These medications improve heart failure symptoms and prognosis by mechanisms such as afterload reduction and favorable ventricular remodeling. 7. Common side effects of ACE inhibitors include dry cough and angioedema. 8. Patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis or severe renal impairment are not suitable candidates for ACE inhibitors. 9. For example, lisinopril can be initiated at 5 mg daily during or after diuresis, with the dose increased every 1-2 weeks to a target dose of 15-20 mg daily. 10. ACE inhibitors are initiated before beta-blockers because they achieve hemodynamic effects more rapidly and are less likely to cause hemodynamic decline. 11. Although some data suggest aspirin may blunt the hemodynamic effects of ACE inhibitors, there is no evidence that aspirin reduces their clinical efficacy in heart failure patients. 12. Aspirin should be given to patients with ischemic heart disease but not to those without it. 13. If a patient cannot tolerate an ACE inhibitor due to a cough, an angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) can be used as a substitute. 14. ARBs block the activation of angiotensin II AT1 receptors, leading to vasodilation, reduced vasopressin secretion, and decreased aldosterone production. 15. Unlike ACE inhibitors, ARBs do not inhibit the breakdown of bradykinin, making them less likely to cause persistent dry cough or angioedema. 16. Commonly used ARBs in heart failure management include candesartan, valsartan, telmisartan, losartan, irbesartan, and olmesartan. 17. The effectiveness of switching from an ACE inhibitor to an ARB was demonstrated in the CHARM-Alternative trial for candesartan. 18. In general, ARBs are as effective or slightly less effective than ACE inhibitors in treating congestive heart failure. 19. It is a Class 2a recommendation to substitute an ARB for an ACE inhibitor if the patient is already taking an ARB for another indication. 20. The efficacy of adding an ARB to an ACE inhibitor was assessed in the CHARM-Added trial, which showed a reduction in the composite primary endpoint but no reduction in mortality. 21. The VALIANT trial demonstrated that an ARB should not be added to an ACE inhibitor in the post-myocardial infarction setting. 22. In contrast, the EMPHASIS-HF trial showed that adding eplerenone (an aldosterone antagonist) to ACE inhibition improved clinical outcomes, including mortality, in patients with Class II or III heart failure and reduced LVEF. 23. Based on the mortality benefit observed in the EMPHASIS-HF trial, an aldosterone antagonist should be added to an ACE inhibitor in patients with NYHA Class II heart failure and LVEF <30%, post-MI patients with LVEF <40% and heart failure symptoms or diabetes, and Class III or IV heart failure patients with LVEF <35%. 24. Triple therapy combining an ACE inhibitor, an ARB, and an aldosterone antagonist is relatively contraindicated. 25. Beta-blockers reduce heart rate, thereby lowering myocardial energy expenditure. 26. They also prolong diastolic filling and increase the duration of coronary perfusion. 27. Beta-blockers reduce the toxic effects of catecholamines on the myocardium. 28. Once a stable dose of a diuretic and an ACE inhibitor is achieved, one of the three beta-blockers associated with improved survival (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, or bisoprolol) can be added, with the dose titrated based on patient tolerance. 29. Beta-blockers with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (e.g., pindolol or acebutolol) should be avoided. 30. Meta-analyses of beta-blockers in heart failure show a 35% reduction in one-year mortality when these drugs are added to ACE inhibitors. 31. While there are no direct comparisons of beta-blockers, some data suggest carvedilol may improve LVEF more than others but may be less well-tolerated due to its vasodilatory properties. 32. Patients who have been over-diuresed may not tolerate the addition of a beta-blocker. 33. Contraindications to beta-blocker initiation include asthma or bronchospasm, hypotension with poor end-organ perfusion, bradycardia or heart block, peripheral arterial disease with limb ischemia at rest, significant peripheral edema, and recent intravenous inotropic therapy. 34. Given the potential for hemodynamic decompensation, beta-blocker initiation is best managed by a specialist or center experienced in heart failure management. 35. Patients should be informed about potential side effects and understand that it may take 1-3 months for beta-blockers to improve heart failure symptoms. 36. Therapy should begin with very low doses, doubling the dose every two weeks until the target dose is reached or symptoms prevent further escalation. 37. Initial and target doses for beta-blockers are as follows: Carvedilol: Initial dose 3.125 mg twice daily, target dose 25-50 mg twice daily. Metoprolol succinate: Initial dose 12.5 mg daily, target dose 200 mg daily. Bisoprolol: Initial dose 1.25 mg daily, target dose 5-10 mg daily. 38. Weight gain or peripheral edema unresponsive to diuresis may require a reduction in beta-blocker dose. 39. An aldosterone antagonist can be added to the regimen of select patients with heart failure. 40. These selected patients include those with Class II heart failure and LVEF <30%, Class III/IV heart failure and LVEF <35%, and post-STEMI patients with LVEF <40% who have symptomatic heart failure or diabetes. 41. Serum potassium must be below 5.0 mEq/L, and the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) should be >30 cc/min for aldosterone antagonist therapy. 42. Renal function and potassium levels must be carefully monitored when using aldosterone antagonists. 43. Eplerenone has fewer endocrine side effects (1%) compared to spironolactone (10%) but is more expensive. 44. A reasonable strategy is to start therapy with spironolactone at 25-50 mg daily and switch to eplerenone at 25-50 mg daily if endocrine side effects develop. 45. Risk factors for hyperkalemia with aldosterone antagonists include triple therapy with an ACE inhibitor and an ARB, which makes this combination contraindicated.
